conversation.content:
Good morning! I’m so glad we’re able to speak today. My name is Dr. Ramirez, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician—my whole focus is on supporting mothers in the weeks and months after birth.  

I’d like to spend a few minutes with the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS. It’s a brief, well-studied questionnaire that helps us understand how you’ve been feeling emotionally and physically over the past seven days. There are no right or wrong answers, and everything you share stays confidential within your care team. My goal is simply to create a safe, judgment-free space where you can tell me how things are really going.  

We’ll go through 10 questions, one at a time, and I’ll ask each in everyday language so it feels conversational. When you’re ready, we can begin.  

To start: Over the past seven days, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

Morning, Dr. Ramirez… I guess I can still laugh sometimes—like when my baby makes those little sleepy smiles—but most of the time it feels kind of forced. I’ll chuckle if my husband jokes, yet the next second I’m tired again and the humor just slips away. So, yes, it’s been harder than it used to be.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Hmm… I’d say “yes, but only sometimes.” I can laugh here and there—like when my little one makes those silly faces while sleeping—but mostly I have to push myself, and the laughter fades fast.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really… I mean, I still plan little outings—like taking the baby for a walk or grabbing coffee with a friend—but when the time comes, I feel kind of “meh.” I go through the motions more than actually feeling excited. Even simple stuff I used to enjoy, like reading or a favorite show, just seems flat lately.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I catch myself doing that. If the baby’s extra fussy, I immediately wonder if it’s something I ate, or if I’m just not soothing him right. Little stuff—like dropping a burp cloth or running late—makes me think, “Ugh, I can’t even handle basic things.” I know it’s probably not fair, but those thoughts still pop in.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

A lot of the time. Even when everything seems fine, I get this knot in my stomach—like I’m waiting for something bad to happen. I’ll check that he’s breathing a hundred times, or worry the bottle temp is wrong, even though I know he’s okay. It’s like my mind won’t settle.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Sometimes. It’s not every day, but a few times this week I’ll be sitting on the couch, everything quiet, and suddenly my heart’s racing and I feel like I can’t get a full breath. There’s no real reason—it just hits and then fades after a few minutes, but it leaves me shaky.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yeah… most of the time it feels like I’m barely treading water. Dishes pile up, laundry never ends, and every time I start one task the baby cries and I lose momentum. I keep thinking, “I should be able to handle this,” but by afternoon I’m just exhausted and want to sit in the quiet and stare at the wall.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

It’s not really sadness keeping me up—more like my mind won’t shut off. I’ll lie down, think about everything I didn’t finish, worry I missed something with the baby, replay every little fussy spell. I finally drift off, but then I jolt awake at every squeak from the crib. So, yeah, several nights this week I’ve stared at the ceiling way too long.
I have felt sad or miserable

Yes, quite often. I wouldn’t say it’s every minute, but most days there’s this heavy, gray feeling that just sits on me. I’ll be feeding the baby and suddenly feel like I could cry—though I usually don’t—then it lifts for a bit and comes back later. It’s like a cloud that keeps drifting in.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Not exactly. I feel teary a lot—like there’s pressure behind my eyes—but I’ve only actually cried once or twice this week, and it was short. Mostly I swallow it down because I’m scared once I start I won’t stop, and the baby needs me.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—never. I might feel overwhelmed, but hurting myself hasn’t crossed my mind. I just want to feel like “me” again so I can take care of my baby.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 19: **Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note**

**Identified Symptoms / Concerns**  
- Persistent low mood, described as “heavy, gray feeling” most days  
- Marked anhedonia: activities planned but experienced as flat; laughter short-lived  
- Excessive self-blame and guilt over minor childcare issues  
- Chronic, ill-defined anxiety (“knot in stomach”), frequent catastrophic worries about infant safety  
- Episodic panic symptoms (sudden racing heart, breathlessness) without clear trigger  
- Overwhelmed/cannot cope: household tasks accumulate, “barely treading water”  
- Mood-related insomnia: difficulty falling/staying asleep linked to ruminative worry  
- Subjective tearfulness, though only one-two brief crying episodes this week  
- No self-harm ideation reported  

**Pattern Summary**  
Consistent with moderate depressive and comorbid anxiety symptoms emerging postpartum. No current safety concerns.

**Screening Significance**  
Meets clinical threshold for further assessment for postpartum depression and possible comorbid anxiety disorder; does not meet criteria for immediate psychiatric emergency (no suicidal intent). Recommend formal evaluation with standardized tool (e.g., PHQ-9, GAD-7, EPDS) and referral for appropriate outpatient treatment/services.
